name: Facial Diplegia with Paresthesias
aliases: Bilateral Facial Paralysis with Sensory Disturbances

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Facial Diplegia with Paresthesias Diagnostic Criteria

criteria.description: Bilateral facial nerve palsy with symmetrical weakness
Presence of distal limb paresthesias or sensory disturbances
No evidence of limb weakness or other cranial nerve involvement
Nerve conduction studies showing demyelinating sensory neuropathy

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Bilateral facial nerve palsy plus distal limb paresthesias with supportive nerve conduction studies; exclusion of other causes
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis requires exclusion of other causes of bilateral facial palsy such as Lyme disease, sarcoidosis, and Guillain-Barré syndrome variants.

pathognomonic.notes: Symmetrical weakness of facial muscles on both sides
Numbness and tingling sensations in hands and feet

searchTerms: loss of eye blink reflex both eyes
absent corneal reflex on both sides

common.notes: Reduced sensation to touch and pinprick
searchTerms: reduced sensation in hands and feet

common.notes: Unsteady gait due to sensory disturbances
searchTerms: mild ataxia in arms and legs

common.notes: Taste disturbances due to chorda tympani involvement

searchTerms: mild weakness in hands and feet

occasional.notes: Increased sensitivity to sound due to stapedius muscle paralysis
Light sensitivity secondary to incomplete eyelid closure
Due to impaired lacrimal gland innervation

rare.notes: Severe cases may involve respiratory compromise
searchTerms: difficulty breathing due to muscle weakness

rare.notes: Includes orthostatic hypotension and cardiac arrhythmias

laboratory: Cerebrospinal fluid showing albuminocytologic dissociation (elevated protein with normal cell count)
Elevated inflammatory markers may be present
imaging: MRI brain typically normal or may show enhancement of facial nerves
Nerve conduction studies demonstrating demyelinating sensory neuropathy
other: Electromyography showing reduced facial nerve motor unit potentials
Negative infectious and autoimmune serologies to exclude mimics

distinguishingFeatures: Elevated CSF protein with clinical progression
History of tick exposure or erythema migrans rash
Often unilateral facial palsy but can be bilateral
Systemic granulomatous disease with multisystem involvement

redFlags: Bilateral facial paralysis with limb weakness or sensory loss
Signs of central nervous system involvement (e.g., altered consciousness, seizures)
references: Ropper AH. Facial diplegia with paresthesias: a variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome. Neurology. 1994.
Hughes RA, Cornblath DR. Guillain-Barré syndrome. Lancet. 2005.
